title: We come to you
hookLine: mourners sit seven days and the community comes to them
carry: none spake a word unto him

cards: The front door is unlatched. Inside, the mirrors are covered and the family sits on low chairs. People come in without ringing, set food down on the kitchen counter, and sit, sometimes without saying anything at all.
This is shiva, the week Jewish mourners keep at home after a funeral. The mourners don't go out to the world. The world comes to them.

teach.b: First, the seven days. The custom reaches back into scripture. When Joseph buried his father Jacob, Genesis says simply, "he made a mourning for his father seven days."

Second, the friends. When Job lost his children, his health and nearly everything else, his friends came and sat with him on the ground for seven days and nights, and the book says "none spake a word unto him."
Before they ever argued with him, they sat. Third, the house. During shiva, mourners sit low, close to the ground.

In some homes the mirrors are covered. The mourners don't cook or host; visitors bring the meals. Prayer services are often held right in the living room, so the mourner can say the Kaddish without leaving home.
Tradition teaches that visitors should let the mourner speak first. If the mourner wants to talk about the person who died, you listen. If not, you sit.
On the way out, visitors often say a traditional line asking that God comfort the mourner among the mourners of Zion and Jerusalem. Grief can shut a person in. Shiva reverses the direction.
The one in pain doesn't have to find the strength to go anywhere or say anything.
The community walks in the door, carrying soup, and says, without words: we come to you.

how: After a funeral, Jewish mourners sit shiva at home, on low seats, while friends and neighbors visit, bring meals, join prayer services in the house, and offer a traditional word of comfort as they leave.

games.q: you walk into a shiva house. the mourner is on a low chair, quiet. what does tradition teach you to do?
o: fill the silence with cheerful talk.
sit down, and let the mourner speak first.
games.why: let the mourner lead. if they want to talk about the person who died, listen. if not, sit with them.

practice: Let someone who is carrying a loss come to mind, a loss this week or one from years ago that still aches, and gently picture how you could come to them: a visit, a call, a message that says you're thinking of them.
You don't need the right words; a shiva visitor may say almost nothing. And if you're the one grieving, think instead of one person you'd let come.

wordCard.voice: Shiva: the week of mourning Jewish families keep at home after a funeral, when the community comes to them. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: shiva, the name for the seven days of mourning at home.

carryVoice: Your line: none spake a word unto him. Sitting came before speaking. See you tomorrow.
